resources.string: Human liver glycogen and glucose research
How glucagon helps the liver release glucose
One pathway through liver glycogen. Thresholds, rates, and personal glucose are not modeled.
When blood glucose falls, pancreatic alpha cells can release more glucagon. Other islet cells help regulate the response.
Alpha cells release stored glucagon into the surrounding tissue, and it enters nearby capillaries.
Glucagon reaches the liver in the bloodstream and signals through a receptor on the hepatocyte surface. It does not turn into glucose.
Receptor signaling promotes glycogen breakdown. Several cellular steps yield free glucose that can enter the blood. The liver also has other glucose-producing pathways.
Free glucose can leave hepatocytes through transporters and enter the blood, helping maintain the glucose supply.
An eccrine gland example. The comparison starts with equal amounts of sweat and does not estimate temperature, fluid loss, or hydration needs.
A nerve signal reaches the gland
The temperature regulation system can signal eccrine glands through sympathetic nerves, stimulating the coiled gland to secrete fluid.
The secretory coil moves salt and water into the lumen. The resulting fluid travels up the duct toward the skin surface.
As fluid flows through the duct, some sodium and chloride are reabsorbed. The remaining liquid continues toward the pore.
Sweat emerges at the skin surface
Sweat emerges through a pore and forms droplets or a film. Liquid on the skin is not yet evaporative cooling.
Evaporating sweat takes heat from the skin. With other conditions equal, humid air usually slows evaporation; more sweat does not always mean more cooling.
